Billy Evans, Holmes’ partner, and Seyfried get into a contentious discussion over dinner about Evans’ attitude toward Holmes. Evans, who has started talking about the box office hit more and more both in interviews and in a Reddit AMA , recently spoke about the visit, and it turns out he didn’t see what was coming at all. In fact, he thought he was extending a peace offering to Seyfried after her portrayal of Holmes in The Dropout .

Seyfried had already been working with Fielder for some time, and over the course of the second half of the movie, it’s clear she was getting more and more frustrated with Evans as she learned more about him. In fact, she was so upset by Evans’ behavior in the footage she had watched with Fielder that was filmed before Holmes reported to prison in 2023, that she expressed a desire to break the couple up. Evans recently told his side of the story to The Hollywood Reporter , saying of the dinner:

It made more sense to me after seeing the film, and hearing her say, ‘I want to break them up.’ I didn’t understand her intentions [when she came over]. I thought we were extending an olive branch and saying, ‘Look, we’re not angry with you. We’re happy to engage. We don’t blame you for your portrayal of Liz [in The Dropout]. You’re an actress, you didn’t write the script, you didn’t develop the story, you didn’t do the research or lack thereof.’

Seyfried’s intentions were never to ask for forgiveness for playing Holmes at this point. At this point, Amanda Seyfried isn't just the actress who portrayed Holmes. She is also an advocate for her. That’s even more apparent when she plays her again later in the documentary, in the recreations of Fielder’s meetings with the former CEO in the Texas prison. Seyfried had, at that point, developed sympathy for Holmes, which is weirdly exactly what Evans was hoping the film would do, though probably not at his expense. Not like this.

It’s impossible to rank all the wildest moments in You Can See Everything . The more I’ve thought about it over the weeks since I saw it, the more each scene stands out from the others. One day I think Evans taking the bowl of eggs out of Holmes' hand is the craziest; other times it's when Holmes seemingly doesn’t understand “Who’s on First?” That’s not even getting into the disputed scene that features Evans in the shower . However, the dinner confrontation is when I was squirming the most in my seat.

Seyfried pulls no punches in telling Evans what she thinks, and in turn, Evans doesn’t hold back his contempt, either. It’s a scene I can’t wait to watch again when I’m finally able to see the movie on streaming, presumably with my HBO Max subscription , soon.

articles.title: Can Peter Rice Fix Netflix? New Content Boss Has a Daunting To-Do List
articles.summary: Ted Sarandos’ handpicked consigliere is tasked with reinventing the streamer — while his boss promises Wall Street that nothing is changing.
articles.content:
Reed Hastings found about Netflix 's big shake-up the same time everyone else did. The Netflix founder (he officially exited the board over the summer) told a rapt audience at the Masters of Scale Summit in San Francisco in late October that the mass layoffs, the exit of content chief Bela Bajaria and the surprise announcement of Peter Rice as its new head of content caught him just as off guard as the rest of Hollywood. "I didn't know those were coming, and it's hard because I'd like to be in the fray helping," Hastings told the audience in the Presidio Theater.

Still, the man who shaped Netflix into today's behemoth had thoughts on what Rice and co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters need to do. "The strategy is doing more and better television shows, more and better movies," Hastings said. "The core brand property is about being thrilling. We realized — it took a long time — that we could be distrusted, we could be disliked, but we can never be boring."

Now the burden will be on Rice to find those thrilling additions to Netflix's menu, perhaps retiring the safe but aging gourmet cheeseburger of the Bajaria era.

Rice helped forge Fox into an entertainment giant and was one of only a few Fox veterans brought into the Disney fold when the assets were acquired under Bob Iger (Disney exec Dana Walden was another). His taste and relationships at both Fox and Disney were, in the words of one source, "exquisite," with a knack for fare that was both commercial and high-end. At Disney, he helped build a general entertainment business from near-scratch, leaning on both FX and Hulu to help it do so.

But he has been out of the corporate mix since Bob Chapek unceremoniously ousted him in 2022, just a few short months before Chapek himself would get the boot.

Those post-corporate gigs, however, shed light on what he can bring to Netflix: He helped the L.A. Olympics Committee develop the entertainment for the opening and closing ceremonies, critical events that will be seen by millions (and perhaps billions) before passing the baton to Kathleen Kennedy. And perhaps more intriguingly, he inked a deal with A24. As A24 was revving up its original productions — thanks to several rounds of investment that ended with a $3.5 billion valuation — the insular New York indie studio signed Rice to a film and TV pact.

It's a testament to Rice's talent relationships that the notoriously director-driven studio tapped him to help shepherd some big swings. His credits at the studio included the Alex Garland-produced Warfare and Chris Rock's return to the director's chair with Misty Green . When he left for his Netflix post, his development slate included A24's biggest production to date, Garland's adaptation of the fantasy video game Elden Ring . In other words, he sought to bridge the highbrow and the mainstream with fare that thrills. It's a skill set that Sarandos seems to admire. "His creative instincts and business acumen are remarkable," Sarandos said to analysts Oct. 20. "Most importantly, Peter Rice understands talent relations."

But Rice will have his work cut out for him thanks in no small part to Sarandos, who keeps a tight leash on Netflix's content output and who already reiterated that the company's content strategy isn't changing. "The business and the business flywheel are working. There's no need for a fundamental shift in strategy," he said, even as he lamented the "doubles and singles" that the company delivered this year. Sarandos wants home runs, and he thinks Rice can do that, with a particular emphasis on the U.S. market.

"These big moves, after a disappointing 2026 in which programming expense grew by 10 percent while U.S. engagement per sub roughly stagnated, admit a problem that is increasingly obvious," Wolfe Research analyst Peter Supino wrote Oct. 20. "Ask a friend whether they are watching more or less Netflix these days — in our experience, they'll say less."

If Rice makes an impact at Netflix in the near term, it may be with the company's film strategy, sources say, with the top job now open with the exit of Dan Lin. Rumors have circulated that ousted Warner Bros. film co-chiefs Pam Abdy and Mike De Luca could be in line to succeed Lin to lead Netflix's film division. But Rice has been telling staff that he isn't hiring a film boss for now. He wants to be in the trenches creatively, multiple sources say.

"We view [the executive changes] as a signal that management is focused on improving content output and creative hit rates," Bank of America analyst Jessia Reif Ehrlich wrote Oct. 21, adding that "management appears increasingly focused on generating larger scale hits in [the U.S. and Canada]. We believe it will take some time before any of the new management changes impact the film or TV slate."

In the meantime, junior executives at Netflix have been calling his former colleagues, asking how to thrive in a Peter Rice meeting. He has strong opinions but can be hard to read. "He'll make you work for it," notes one former colleague of his style, which involves leaving subordinates to figure out the solution without him spelling it out.

While Netflix is a major player in the movie business, it has largely avoided theatrical. Sarandos has said the company has not changed its streaming-first mentality, but rival film executives believe that a year from now, many more of the company's movies will have a theatrical component, à la Amazon.

That's easier said than done. The company has relied on its algorithm — not its marketing — for the vast majority of its successes. But the company has conspicuously changed its tune of late: Netflix users have noticed that it now runs teaser trailers for its shows before other Netflix programming, a classic TV marketing move it has long shunned. And the company launched a major brand campaign dubbed "Find the Thing You Never Knew You Needed" on connected TVs, YouTube, TikTok and other platforms — as well as in movie theaters. The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth (Nov. 25) and Narnia: The Magician's Nephew (Feb. 12) will be key tests to see if Netflix's marketing department can get people to theaters. Rivals believe they'll need to make more hires with theatrical marketing experience if they want to make a real go of it.

After Netflix failed to acquire Warner Bros. and its library, including DC Comics, Rice will also need to beef up its homegrown IP, particularly on the film side. "Netflix is weak in long-lasting franchises and universes," notes one veteran film exec known for IP plays. "Ted says he wants to have big, culturally impactful successes — and maybe universes. What's then the next chess moves on that? They don't have Marvel or DC, and there's not one big acquisition to do it. How do they navigate that and show Wall Street and the entertainment world they can build what they weren't able acquire?""

Of course, Comcast is set to imminently spin off NBCUniversal, raising buzz in Hollywood as to whether the streaming giant may make one more acquisition play in search of franchises and film expertise. In a note to NBCUniversal staff Nov. 16, CEO Mike Cavanagh touted the "open, partnership-driven approach" that the company has, which "allows us to go even further, bringing great content to consumers wherever and however they choose to engage."

Indeed, one critique of Netflix over the past few years is that some of its biggest hits caught it by surprise, leaving it scrambling to catch up when Squid Game and KPop Demon Hunters hit big. In both instances, the company scrambled to secure Halloween costumes or merchandise for fans, deals that typically would be locked up well before a debut of a series or film. It's a sore spot Sarandos is well aware of. Earlier this year, the co-CEO oversaw the launch of a branding effort dubbed "The Netflix Effect," which attempted to calculate the economic and cultural impact of the company.

"Over the last decade, Netflix shows and movies have consistently shaped what people read, buy, listen to, eat, wear and play. We've pushed old songs back up the musical charts, helped niche sports go mainstream, and boosted sales of everything from chess sets, to Halloween costumes, to home storage," Sarandos wrote at the time. "Now we have a responsibility to keep that flywheel going."

Rice may be able to manage that flywheel better, but "let's only make the hits" is a running joke in Hollywood. Still, Hastings may be on to something. Rice may not be able to guarantee hits, but his track record suggests he can guarantee buzz. Whatever happens next, it won't be boring.

Borys Kit and Aaron Couch contributed to this report.

articles.title: 'SmartLess' Trio to Back 'Small Town Narcos' Podcast (Exclusive)
articles.summary: The partnership with New Metric Media will produce a Chris Kelly-hosted true-crime comedy podcast about Canada's largest drug sting.
articles.content:
SmartLess hosts and creators Jason Bateman, Will Arnett and Sean Hayes are partnering with Canadian indie studio New Metric Media and the CBC, the country's public broadcaster, on a true-crime comedy podcast series, Small Town Narcos, to be hosted by Chris Kelly.

The six-part Canadian series, to premiere globally in Feb. 2027, will center on a 1989 drug sting in the province of New Brunswick, and combine a real-time investigation, interviews with retired Mounties and cartel lawyers, archival materials and dramatic recreations. The podcast will recount two Colombian cartel pilots crash-landing a plane half-filled with Pablo Escobar's cocaine into the New Brunswick woods, only to be arrested by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) after a tip-off and in place to make the country's largest-ever drug bust.

The drama to follow included a foiled jailbreak plot, a daylight assassination, a Supreme Court case argued in secret and an RCMP informant who had infiltrated the cartel. Small Town Narcos , to launch at On Air Fest in Brooklyn, follows on a stable of comedic podcasts from Smartless Media that includes the mega-hit SmartLess , Just Jack & Will, Bad Dates and Owned.

Kelly, while hosting and executive producing the Canadian podcast, is also vp of podcasts at New Metric Media, the producer of Letterkenny and the spinoff Shoresy that has also branched out into podcasts, gaming and other digital media ventures.

"I grew up in a corner of Canada where I was sure nothing exciting had ever happened. Then I found out that for one stretch of 1989, it was the most exciting place on earth. It's like learning your boring parents were secretly spies!" Kelly said in a statement. "As we launch New Metric Podcasts, we're looking to create exactly these kinds of stories – original ideas, distinctive creative voices and unexpected worlds that can connect with audiences in a big way. Small Town Narcos is a great example of what we want to build, and we're excited to bring it to life with our incredible partners at CBC and SmartLess Media."

Small Town Narcos, written by Kelly and Eunice Kim, is produced by SmartLess Media and New Metric Media for the CBC. The executive producer credits are shared by Arnett, Bateman, Hayes, Richard Korson, Bernie Kaminski, Mark Montefiore, Kelly, Chris Okea and Cesil Fernandes, with Kim serving as senior producer.

articles.title: 5 Metropolis Disasters That Make Gotham's Worst Nightmares Look Like a Good Day
articles.summary: Image Courtesy of DC Comics If you ask anyone what the worst city to live in DC would be, odds are that they'd tell you it was Gotham eleven out of ten times. It's true that Gotham has about every problem under the sun and then some, but its horrible reputation actually masks just how terrible it would be to […]
articles.content:
Accurately named, this story was one of the darkest days for the City of Tomorrow. It took place across nine issues of every Superman title in 1994, covering both the “Battle for Metropolis” and “Fall of Metropolis.” To keep it brief, Lex Luthor was inhabiting a clone body that was breaking down, and when he realized that nothing could save him, he decided to unleash his scorched-earth policy to ensure that, if he went down, he'd at least bring all of Metropolis down with him. He set off missiles across the city that reduced most of its buildings to rubble, unleashed killer robots to hunt down any survivors, trapped everyone in visions of their worst fears with a hallucinogenic fog cloud, and even piloted a Kryptonian Warsuit to try and finally bring Superman down.

This is Lex at his most bloodthirsty and destructive , driven by nothing but vanity and a sick sense to leave his mark on the world, even if that be through petty revenge on the people he felt spurned him. Superman, Superboy, and Supergirl managed to save whoever they could, but Metropolis was wrecked like it had never been before or since. As if all of that wasn't enough, Lex wound up making a deal with Neron for a healthy body, so none of this mattered, anyways. One man's tantrum nearly brought down millions of lives, and there's no better story that shows how corrupt but connected Luthor is with Metropolis.

The “Darkseid War” event saw two of the Justice League's greatest villains clash as Darkseid and the Anti-Monitor came to blows, and in the ensuing scramble to save whoever they could, each Leaguer found a path towards divinity. Justice League: Darkseid War – Superman tells about how the newly dubbed God of Strength returned to Metropolis, only to find another alien attacking it to do something with the Man of Tomorrow that remains unclear. However, his weapon was pretty straightforward. After losing to Superman in a fight, the alien infected all of Metropolis with a black ooze that covered and blotted out everything and everyone, leaving them in a kind of horrific stasis. In minutes, it took over the entire city, leaving only Superman.

Superman saved the day, of course, but what this incident really highlights is that alien invasions like this aren't anything out of the ordinary. This wasn't treated like some horrible tragedy that everyone would remember for years, as stuff like this happens in Metropolis all the time. Even Superman calls out how formulaic this type of thing is. Really sit with that. An alien unleashed a black ooze that trapped everyone in the city in minutes, but that's so average that after Superman averts it you just go about your day. The fact that this sort of thing is commonplace in Metropolis says everything it needs to about how absolutely insane its daily life is, and it's nothing good.

This five-part storyline, taking place from Action Comics #1017 to #1021, saw Superman's greatest villains bring war to Metropolis. The mysterious and maniacal Leviathan, the untouchable Red Cloud, and the Apex Lex Luthor and his Legion of Doom joined forces to bring Metropolis to its knees and take over the world, colliding with the Justice League and Young Justice squarely in the middle of the City of Tomorrow. Any one of these heroes and villains could cause some pretty serious damage on their own, but when everyone was throwing punches and lasers at everyone else, it became a bloodbath. Most of Metropolis was left in ruins, and the villains all escaped, meaning that there wasn't even any resolution beyond survival.

This story might not have had the lasting impact that “Fall of Metropolis” had, but it did show just how many players had their eyes set on Superman's fair city. Three distinct groups with their own goals, all able to hold their own or even outright bring down Superman, decided to work together and show everyone that the only thing holding these villains back some days is their own inability to trust each other. If they all worked together, not even Superman would be able to stop them. Everyone has their eyes on Metropolis. It's DC's shining jewel, but that means that everyone wants to own it.

Without a doubt, the biggest and bloodiest battle in this city's history was the Battle of Metropolis. It came about in the pages of Infinite Crisis . Seeing that his plans to create the perfect Earth failed, Alexander Luthor decided to conquer New Earth and remake it in his image. To that end, his Society broke every superpowered villain out of jail and unleashed them like an army on Metropolis, hoping to make it Alexander's first capture in his crusade. Dozens, if not hundreds, of villains appeared in Metropolis with no plan beyond wanton destruction, and so the entire superhero community joined forces to combat them. It would be easier to list everyone who wasn't present for this gargantuan brawl, and you can imagine just how destructive it was.

This fight, just as “Metropolis Doom!” did, showed that Metropolis has become the center point of DC's Earth, with every villain aiming to make it their own. This was about a hundred times more destructive, as it involved far too many characters to name, all pushed to their breaking point long before this actually went down. The battle also served as the ultimate showcase of just how dark comics had become in the Infinite Crisis era, dealing out death and blood like there was no tomorrow, because it treated it like there might not be. This was the costume fight to end all fights, and there's no comparison for just how much it destroyed.

The final Metropolis tragedy is much less impactful and showy than the previous, but is altogether more insidious. Lex Luthor despised Superman for, in his own words, stealing his city from him, so he decided the greatest payback was to prove that Superman couldn't handle everything. Lex unleashed a viral bacteria that infected all of Metropolis but LexCorp and Superman himself, leaving everyone stricken with fevers that would kill them soon enough. He forced Superman to work with Toxin, the Man of Steel's biggest fangirl, to distribute the antidote, but the strain wound up killing her. Superman saved Metropolis, but Lex showed him that his actions would always come at a price that Lex would force him to pay.

This isn't an alien invasion or a massive hero-villain brawl. This is the twisted will of one spiteful man , who chose to risk every life in Metropolis to prove that he could hurt Superman whenever he wanted. Lex can and will use everyone in Metropolis as a pawn for his schemes, all out of some twisted sense of love and ego. Just living in Metropolis makes you a target and potential mark, and Lex is just as powerful today as he was when this was released. Living in Metropolis means living at Lex Luthor's mercy, and there are few things as terrifying as that.

Which of Metropolis's major disasters do you think left the biggest impact on the city? Let us know in the comments below!

articles.content:
Qatar 's Film Committee, the body overseeing the development of the country's film and TV business, is gearing up for the second edition of its Industry Days, running from November 19 to 20 alongside the Doha Film Festival .

The inaugural edition unveiled long-gestated plans with a bang last year. Alongside a 50% film and TV cash rebate, the event also announced plans to shoot a contemporary Barbara Broccoli-produced version of Othello starring David Oyelowo and Cynthia Erivo in the Gulf state as well as partnerships with Neon, Company 3, Miramax, Department M and Sony. Related Stories News Festival In Focus: Qatar Ramps Up International Film & TV Ambitions As Local Talent Shines News Festival In Focus: Doha Gears Up For Lift-Off Against Geopolitical Odds: "It's Not Smaller, We Have More Films & Guests"

DEADLINE: What was the feedback after the first edition of the Industry days?

HASSAN AL-THAWADI : The feedback around Industry Days was very encouraging. The first edition gave us an opportunity to introduce our vision for Qatar's film industry, engage the region and hear directly from filmmakers, studios, producers and financiers.

More importantly, after the event, we understood that our vision resonated with support for the ecosystem around financing, production, talent, infrastructure and access to the region we are trying to build.

A year later, our focus is on demonstrating how that vision is taking shape through tangible projects, partnerships and production activity. This edition is about sharing what has moved forward and the progress we have made over the past year, what we have learned, how we have adapted, and what comes next.

DEADLINE: Will this edition feature as many announcements? Can you tease any?

AL-THAWADI: There will be some new announcements, but I will leave the specifics for Doha . The overall message will be very clear: we are moving from vision to execution, building on what we started last year and putting more of the pieces of that ecosystem into place. Ultimately, we are open for business. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dl-mid-article-inject2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article2","mid-articleX","mid-article","mid","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Last year was about introducing the Film Committee, our ambition to transform Qatar into a global hub for the film industry, and a new proposition for the region to create greater opportunities and international visibility for Arab cinemas. This year the emphasis is on progress and moving from ambition into activity.

The clearest evidence of progress this year is a portfolio of supported films with Paper Tiger , Artou and Furie s reaching international festivals, and projects moving through creative development and production planning.

You will hear more about the Qatar Screen Production Incentive and how we are extending its regional reach, about projects and talent moving into their next stages, and about partnerships becoming more practical and production focused.

DEADLINE: In the interim, we've had the U.S.-Israel war on Iran which has had fallout across the Gulf region for business and tourism. How has this impacted your plans at the Film Committee?

AL-THAWADI: We can't escape the difficult period our region has experienced. However, the fundamentals of what we are trying to build has not changed. We have a long-term strategy to attract international production, develop Arab talent and capability and to create a stronger platform for stories from our region to reach global audiences.

DEADLINE: Are companies still interested in setting up here or striking partnerships?

AL-THAWADI: Absolutely. We continue to see strong interest, although I think the nature of the conversation has matured. A year ago, much of the discussion was about the proposition of Qatar.

Today, the conversations are increasingly around specific projects, production activity, financing, services and access to the wider region. We are already seeing that translate into production activity through the Qatar Screen Production Incentive, alongside continued engagement with international studios and production partners.

The objective is not simply to have companies establish a presence in Qatar. For us, what matters most is sustained activity: productions being made, capability being transferred, local and regional talent being developed, and commercial relationships that give companies a reason to continue investing and working here and across the region. That is what we are building, and we continue to see appetite for it.

DEADLINE: Have any productions accessed the rebate?

AL-THAWADI: Yes. We have pilot productions already leveraging the Qatar Screen Production Incentive. Three major production companies are currently using the programme, including a leading global streaming platform, and those productions have already created more than 500 jobs locally, while generating activity for hotels, transport, security, logistics and other suppliers.

For us, the important point is that we are beginning to see the incentive translate into real production activity, jobs and opportunities within Qatar, and now we're extending its reach. We are strengthening regional collaboration and building the infrastructure that is required for global studios to film and produce in countries across the region.

DEADLINE: What's the state of play for ‘ Othello '?

AL-THAWADI : We are still in discussions with our production partner, Eon, and look forward to sharing further developments once confirmed.

DEADLINE: What's your long-term view for Qatar's future as a media and entertainment hub?

We believe Qatar can become both a gateway and a platform that serves as regional hub for the global film and entertainment industry: a gateway connecting talent, creatives and companies from our region to global markets, and a platform where international partners can work with the talent, stories and capabilities of the Arab world. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-articleX","mid-article","btf","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() ; });

My long-term view for Qatar as a hub for the global film and entertainment industry continues to be ambitious, expansive and collaborative. Success for us is not simply how many productions shoot in Qatar. It is whether we build a sustainable ecosystem with the necessary financing, production, post-production, distribution, talent development, technology and infrastructure to create lasting cultural and economic value in Qatar and across the region.

Arab storytelling remains underrepresented globally. Our goal is to help create the conditions for those stories to be developed at the highest level and reach audiences around the world, while at the same time making Qatar a serious and trusted destination for international production.

One of the lessons of the World Cup is that when you invest with a clear long-term purpose, you can build capability and create a legacy that extends far beyond the event itself. Film has that same ability to bring people together and broaden representation. We are still at the beginning of that journey, but the direction is very clear.
